Thistle
THIS-ul
noun
From the Old English thistel, a prickly weed of the field; in Scripture the companion of the thorn, and with it the standing sign of the ground cursed for Adam’s sake.

Biblical Definition

The thistle is a prickly weed — useless, self-seeding, quick to hold ground, hard to root out. Its first appearance in Scripture fixes its meaning for ever, for it is part of the sentence passed in Eden: “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field” (Gen 3:18). The earth itself was cursed for man’s sake, and thistles are the visible proof of it. Every field that must be weeded preaches Genesis 3; the ground gives its increase now only against resistance, and man eats bread in the sweat of his face. From that root the word grows three ways. It is the emblem of pride in Jehoash’s stinging parable to Amaziah: “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle” (2Ki 14:9) — the weed proposed an alliance with the cedar and was trampled by a passing beast, and Amaziah, who would not hear it, was beaten. It is the emblem of a false profession in the LORD’s test of teachers: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Mat 7:16). And it is the emblem of desolation, springing up on the altars of a false worship (Hos 10:8). Nature is uniform: a thistle bears thistles, and a false heart bears its own fruit.

Webster 1828 Definition

A prickly weed of the field; with the thorn, the sign of the ground cursed for man’s sake.

expand to see more

THISTLE, a prickly plant of the fields, of many species, troublesome to the husbandman.

From Old English thistel; in Scripture always coupled with the thorn.

Thorns and thistles are the ground’s answer to Adam’s sin (Gen 3:18).

Jehoash likened proud Amaziah to a thistle courting a cedar (2Ki 14:9).

Men do not gather figs of thistles: the fruit declares the tree (Mat 7:16).

Key Scripture

Gen 3:18 — "Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;"

2Ki 14:9 — "And Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle."

Job 31:40 — "Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended."

Hos 10:8 — "The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us."

Modern Corruption

A weed whose testimony is denied — for if there was no historical fall, the thistle is simply nature, and the world is as God first made it.

expand to see more

The corruption here is not linguistic but doctrinal: the denial of a historical Adam and a real curse. Theistic evolution and its evangelical borrowers must read Genesis 3 as a parable of the human condition, which means the thorns and thistles were always there, that thistle and famine and death belong to the world as God pronounced it very good, and that the groaning of the creation Paul describes (Rom 8:20–22) is not a wound but a design. Scripture will not bend to it. The ground was cursed for thy sake, at a moment, because of a man’s sin; the thistle is an intruder in a good creation, not a feature of it. Deny that and you have made God the author of the curse rather than the Judge who pronounced it, and you have cut the nerve of the gospel, for the Last Adam undoes what the first Adam did, and if the first Adam did nothing there is nothing to undo.

Three lessons stand once the doctrine is held. First, labour is now against resistance, and the sweat of the face is part of the sentence — which is why every honest day’s work is a small preaching of Genesis 3 and a small groaning after redemption. Second, pride is a thistle: Jehoash’s parable is cruel and true, the weed proposing marriage to the cedar and trodden down by a beast that never noticed it, and Amaziah lost his kingdom refusing the lesson. Third, fruit is the test of profession — men do not gather figs of thistles, and no confession of orthodoxy, no warmth of manner, no crowd, can make a corrupt tree bear good fruit. Yet the curse has a limit and a term. The Man who wore the thorns of Adam’s curse upon His head bore the whole sentence, and in the day of His appearing the ground itself is delivered: instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle tree (Isa 55:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A prickly field-weed; with the thorn, the standing sign of the curse on the ground.

expand to see more

Thistle — Old English thistel, a prickly weed of the fields.

First named in the sentence on the ground: thorns also and thistles (Gen 3:18).

It is the intruder in a good creation, not a part of its original design.

Jehoash’s parable makes it the emblem of pride overreaching (2Ki 14:9).

Christ makes it the test of teachers: no figs grow on thistles (Mat 7:16).

Usage

"Thorns also and thistles — every weeded field preaches Genesis 3."

"The thistle courted the cedar and was trodden down: pride overreaching itself."

"Do men gather figs of thistles? The fruit, not the profession, declares the tree."
